name: The Bur Oak on the Midway

location.address: Midway Plaisance at Ellis Avenue, Hyde Park, Chicago, IL

story: When the Midway Plaisance was cleared and regraded for the 1893 World's Fair, one tree was left standing, and this is it. By then it was already substantial enough that the ecologist Henry Cowles used it in his 1901 textbook as the example of its kind. Accounts of the fair place it behind the Sitting Bull's Cabin exhibit and the ostrich farm concession, neither of which lasted the year. Sources disagree on how it got here, and it is worth stating both. The University of Chicago Magazine quotes a campus environment official describing it as ostensibly planted as part of a Native American exhibit during the fair itself. The better supported account, from the Hyde Park historian Gary Ossewaarde, from Cowles in 1901 and from a local history record of a 2024 trunk measurement, has it standing long before 1893 and deliberately spared. That measurement reportedly ran past the largest bur oak on the Morton Arboretum's own growth reference chart, which would push it beyond the 250 or so years usually quoted. Bur oak is the tree of the prairie edge in this part of Illinois, corky barked enough to survive the fires that kept the grassland open. This one is the last of that landscape left on the Midway. It stands near Ellis Avenue, in front of the university hospital, on a pin that is close rather than surveyed.
access: Free, public park path along the Midway Plaisance
transport: Metra Electric District to 59th St/University of Chicago station, about 22 minutes from Millennium Station downtown, then a short walk to Ellis Ave and the Midway

name: The Bur Oak Grove of Wooded Island
age_estimate: the grove's oldest survivors are roughly 200 to 300 years

location.address: Wooded Island, Jackson Park, south end near the Clarence Darrow Bridge and Osaka Garden (6200 S. Cornell Ave area), Chicago, IL

story: One of these oaks blew down around 2016, and its rings were counted back to roughly 1730. It had been standing for nearly three centuries when it fell. The ones still up are of the same generation: DNAinfo reported 250 year old bur oaks across the island, with a red oak of about 150 among them. Wooded Island is the part of the 1893 World's Fair that was deliberately left alone. Frederick Law Olmsted kept buildings off it entirely while the Court of Honor went up in white plaster to the south, and fair era painters kept turning their backs on the architecture to paint these oaks instead. The island sits on an undisturbed sand ridge, which is why the soil under the trees was never scraped and rebuilt the way the rest of Jackson Park was. In 2016 the Army Corps of Engineers spent 8.1 million dollars restoring the habitat here and wrote the old bur oaks into the plan, along with roughly 120 bur oak saplings that had seeded themselves around their parents. An oak stand actually reproducing inside a city is a rare thing to stand in. The place to stand is the path just south of the Osaka Garden, looking into the south end of the island, where the grove reads as one thing rather than as scattered trees.

best_time.label: September and October, when the big fringed bur oak acorns come down

access: Free, public park, Chicago Park District (Wooded Island / Osaka Garden)
transport: Metra Electric District to 59th St/University of Chicago station, about 22 minutes from downtown, then roughly a 15 to 20 minute walk east across Jackson Park to Wooded Island; or CTA bus to the Museum of Science and Industry and cross the Clarence Darrow Bridge

name: The Bur Oak Savanna of Union Ridge Cemetery
age_estimate: the oldest estimated at 325 to 375 years, based on trunk size

location.address: Union Ridge Cemetery, 6700 W Higgins Ave, Chicago, IL 60656

story: The oldest oak in this grove has been estimated at 325 to 375 years, which would make it roughly two centuries older than the city around it. It was already a mature prairie tree when Chicago was a portage and a fort. The figure comes from Scott Carlini, quoted in a 2016 hunt for the city's oldest tree, and it is based on trunk diameter rather than a ring core, so treat it as directional. We found no second independent estimate, which is why this entry stays flagged. What is solid is the setting. Union Ridge took its first burial in 1841 and is described by the Norwood Park Historical Society as the oldest continuously operating cemetery in Chicago. The ground was open prairie before it was platted, and what stands here is a genuine relict bur oak savanna: widely spaced, heavy limbed trees with daylight between them, which is what oaks look like when they grow up in grassland rather than in forest. Bur oak's thick corky bark let it survive the fires that kept that prairie open, and the graves that arrived in 1841 put an end to both the fires and the plough. It is a working cemetery, so come during posted visiting hours and behave like a guest. The pin is the entrance; the old section and its oaks are inside the grounds.
access: Free, cemetery grounds open to visitors during posted hours
transport: Metra Union Pacific Northwest Line to Norwood Park station, about 22 minutes from Ogilvie Transportation Center downtown, then a short walk
